title: Why is 0.1 + 0.2 not 0.3?
checkedAgainst: CPython's own float, which `model.test.ts` runs through `oracle/doubles.py` each time: `float.as_integer_ratio` and `decimal.Decimal` for the exact fraction and every decimal digit of several hundred doubles, `math.nextafter` for their neighbours, `repr` for what each prints as, `fractions.Fraction` for the exact sum of two doubles, and float addition and `float()` for what the model's rounding must give. The same test holds the model's rounded sums and stored decimals to JavaScript's own `+` and `Number()` on this machine; `answers.ts` computes the check answers from the model.

questions.question: Is 0.2 + 0.4 == 0.6 true or false, and what does the sum print as?
questions.answer: False: the sum prints as 0.6000000000000001. 0.2 is stored a little high and 0.4 a little high; their exact sum falls exactly halfway between the double 0.6 is stored as and the next one up, and the tie goes to the one whose last bit is 0, the upper.

questions.question: A loop adds 0.1 to a total ten times, starting from 0.1. Is the total 1?
questions.answer: No: it is 0.9999999999999999. Each addition rounds its exact result to a neighbouring double, and over the nine additions the small errors do not cancel. Count in whole numbers (ten tenths) or compare with a tolerance instead of ==.

questions.question: Why does 0.5 + 0.25 == 0.75 hold with no luck involved?
questions.answer: 0.5, 0.25 and 0.75 are a half, a quarter and three quarters: whole numbers over a power of two, so each is stored exactly, their sum is a double already, and nothing is rounded.

steps.title: 0.1 + 0.2 is not 0.3
steps.line: What a language prints for 0.1 + 0.2, for 0.3, and for whether they are equal.
steps.caption: Ask JavaScript or Python for 0.1 + 0.2 and it prints 0.30000000000000004; ask whether that equals 0.3 and it says false. Nothing is broken: every language that uses the processor’s own floating-point numbers says false too. The numbers the machine adds are not quite the ones typed, and the sum is rounded once more.

steps.title: 0.1 is kept as a nearby fraction, a little high
steps.line: A double is a whole number over a power of two.
steps.caption: A double, the machine’s number, holds a whole number divided by a power of two. One tenth is not such a fraction, just as one third has no finite decimal, so the machine keeps the nearest one it can: 3602879701896397 over 2 to the power 55, a little high. 0.2 is kept a little high and 0.3 a little low. Each decimal, and then their sum, is rounded to the nearest number the machine can hold.
steps.picture: 0.1 is kept as exactly 3602879701896397 over 2 to the power 55; 7 labels.

steps.title: 0.3 falls in a gap between two doubles
steps.line: Ticks are doubles; between two ticks there is nothing to keep.
steps.caption: Three neighbouring doubles near 0.3, drawn as ticks. Between ticks there is no number the machine can hold, and the gap here is 2 to the power minus 54, about 0.000000000000000055. The ring marks 0.3 exactly as typed: it falls a fifth of the way across a gap, so it is kept as the nearer tick, the dot.

steps.title: The exact sum falls in the same gap. Which tick will it be kept as?
steps.line: Predict: the same double as 0.3, or a different one?
steps.caption: Now add the two numbers the machine kept for 0.1 and 0.2, exactly, with no rounding. The result, the square, is not a double either: it falls exactly halfway between two ticks. The machine has to keep one of the two. Will it be the tick 0.3 was kept as?

steps.title: The sum is rounded up, one double past 0.3’s
steps.caption: A tie always goes to the tick whose last binary digit is 0, here the upper one. 0.3 was kept as the lower tick. So the machine holds two different doubles, one gap apart, and == compares doubles: false. Typing 0.3 rounded one way, and adding rounded the other.

steps.title: The sum prints as 0.30000000000000004, the shortest name of its double
steps.line: Printing shows the fewest digits that tell a double from its neighbours.
steps.caption: Printing does not show every digit a double holds. It shows the shortest decimal that reads back as the same double and no other. For the double 0.3 is kept as, that is 0.3. The sum’s double is its neighbour, and nothing shorter than 0.30000000000000004 names it without naming another. The extra digits were there all along; they show when two neighbours must be told apart.

steps.title: Whether a sum looks right depends on where it falls
steps.line: Four sums, what each prints as, and whether that is the decimal expected.
steps.caption: Sums of decimals go through the same two roundings; what differs is where the exact sum falls between two doubles. 0.1 + 0.3 rounds onto the double for 0.4, 0.1 + 0.7 rounds to the double below the one for 0.8, and only 0.5 + 0.25 is exact, because halves and quarters are whole numbers over a power of two. So do not test sums of decimals with ==: compare within a tolerance, or count in whole units such as cents.

steps.title: 0.1 + 0.3 == 0.4 is true, but not because the sum is exact
steps.line: What a language prints for 0.1 + 0.3, for 0.4, and for whether they are equal.
steps.caption: Ask JavaScript or Python whether 0.1 + 0.3 equals 0.4 and it says true, yet 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 is false in the same languages. Neither answer is a bug, and every language that uses the processor’s own floating-point numbers gives both. The numbers the machine adds are not quite the ones typed, and the sum is rounded once more. Here the rounding happens to land where 0.4 is kept.
